q-129441.name: Question 1
q-129441.problem: Determine the equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=y\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)$ at the point $(0,-2,0).$
q-129441.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)) \\  & =\frac{2xy}{{x}^{2}+1} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y)=(0,-2):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(0,-2) & =\frac{2(0)(-2)}{{0}^{2}+1}=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(0,-2) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({0}^{2}+1)=0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-0 & =(x-0)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(0,-2)+(y-(-2))\frac{∂f}{∂y}(0,-2) \\ z & =0x+0(y+2) \\ z & =0\end{aligned}
$$

q-37595.name: Question 2
q-37595.problem: Find the equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z={y}^{2}{e}^{2x}-1$ at the point $(0,2,3).$
q-37595.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}{e}^{2x}-1) \\  & =2{y}^{2}{e}^{2x} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}{e}^{2x}-1) \\  & =2y{e}^{2x}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y)=(0,2):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(0,2) & =2(2)^{2}{e}^{2(0)}=8 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(0,2) & =2(2){e}^{2(0)}=4\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-3 & =(x-0)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(0,2)+(y-2)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(0,2) \\ z-3 & =8(x-0)+4(y-2) \\ z-3 & =8x+4y-8 \\ -8x-4y+z+5 & =0 \\ 8x+4y-z-5 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

q-73844.problem: Find the equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z={x}^{3}+x{y}^{2}+{x}^{2}y-{y}^{3}$ at the point $(1,2,-1).$
q-73844.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}+x{y}^{2}+{x}^{2}y-{y}^{3}) \\  & =3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+2xy \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{3}+x{y}^{2}+{x}^{2}y-{y}^{3}) \\  & =2xy+{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y)=(1,2):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,2) & =3(1)^{2}+{2}^{2}+2(1)(2)=11 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,2) & =2(1)(2)+{1}^{2}-3(2)^{2}=-7\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-(-1) & =(x-1)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,2)+(y-2)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,2) \\ z+1 & =11(x-1)-7(y-2) \\ z+1 & =11x-7y+3 \\ -11x+7y+z-2 & =0 \\ 11x-7y-z+2 & =0\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}-{x}^{2}y) \\  & =-2xy \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}-{x}^{2}y) \\  & =2y-{x}^{2}\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,0) & =-2(1)(0)=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,0) & =2(0)-{1}^{2}=-1\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}z-0 & =(x-1)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,0)+(y-0)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,0) \\ z & =0(x-1)-y \\ z & =-y \\ y+z & =0\end{aligned}
$$

q-73849.problem: Find the equation of the tangent hyperplane to the hypersurface $w=2x{y}^{2}+y{z}^{2}-3{x}^{2}z$ at the point $(2,-2,1,2).$
q-73849.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the hypersurface $w=f(x,y,z)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0},{w}_{0})$ on the hypersurface can be written as

$$
w-{w}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(z-{z}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂z}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x{y}^{2}+y{z}^{2}-3{x}^{2}z)=2{y}^{2}-6xz \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x{y}^{2}+y{z}^{2}-3{x}^{2}z)=4xy+{z}^{2} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(2x{y}^{2}+y{z}^{2}-3{x}^{2}z)=2yz-3{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z)=(2,-2,1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(2,-2,1) & =2(-2)^{2}-6(2)(1)=-4 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(2,-2,1) & =4(2)(-2)+(1)^{2}=-15 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z}(2,-2,1) & =2(-2)(1)-3(2)^{2}=-16\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

$$
\begin{aligned}w-2 & =(x-2)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(2,-2,1)+(y+2)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(2,-2,1)+(z-1)\frac{∂f}{∂z}(2,-2,1) \\ w-2 & =-4(x-2)-15(y+2)-16(z-1) \\ w-2 & =-4x+8-15y-30-16z+16 \\ 4x+15y+16z+w+4 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

w−w0=(x−x0)∂f∂x(x0,y0,z0)+(y−y0)∂f∂y(x0,y0,z0)+(z−z0)∂f∂z(x0,y0,z0).

∂f∂x=∂∂x(2xy2+yz2−3x2z)=2y2−6xz∂f∂y=∂∂y(2xy2+yz2−3x2z)=4xy+z2∂f∂z=∂∂z(2xy2+yz2−3x2z)=2yz−3x2

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at (x,y,z)=(2,−2,1):

q-73850.problem: Find the equation of the tangent hyperplane to the hypersurface $w=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{2})$ at the point $(1,-1,1,0).$
q-73850.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the hypersurface $w=f(x,y,z)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0},{w}_{0})$ on the hypersurface can be written as

$$
w-{w}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(z-{z}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂z}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}))=\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}))=\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}))=-\frac{2z}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,-1,1) & =\frac{2(1)}{(1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}-(1)^{2}}=2 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,-1,1) & =\frac{2(-1)}{(1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}-(1)^{2}}=-2 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,-1,1) & =-\frac{2(1)}{(1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}-(1)^{2}}=-2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

$$
\begin{aligned}w-0 & =(x-1)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,-1,1)+(y+1)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,-1,1)+(z-1)\frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,-1,1) \\ w & =2(x-1)-2(y+1)-2(z-1) \\ w & =2x-2-2y-2-2z+2 \\ -2x+2y+2z+w+2 & =0 \\ 2x-2y-2z-w-2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

$$

q-129485.name: Question 9
q-129485.problem: Find the equation of the tangent hyperplane to the hypersurface $w=4x\operatorname{arctan}⁡(yz)$ at the point $(-1,1,1,-\pi ).$
q-129485.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the hypersurface $w=f(x,y,z)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0},{w}_{0})$ on the hypersurface can be written as

$$
w-{w}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(z-{z}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂z}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x\operatorname{arctan}⁡(yz))=4\operatorname{arctan}⁡(yz) \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4x\operatorname{arctan}⁡(yz))=\frac{4xz}{1+{y}^{2}{z}^{2}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(4x\operatorname{arctan}⁡(yz))=\frac{4xy}{1+{y}^{2}{z}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z)=(-1,1,1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(-1,1,1) & =4\operatorname{arctan}⁡(1\cdot 1)=\pi  \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(-1,1,1) & =\frac{4(-1)(1)}{1+({1}^{2})({1}^{2})}=-2 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z}(-1,1,1) & =\frac{4(-1)(1)}{1+({1}^{2})({1}^{2})}=-2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

$$
\begin{aligned}w-(-\pi ) & =(x-(-1))\frac{∂f}{∂x}(-1,1,1)+(y-1)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(-1,1,1)+(z-1)\frac{∂f}{∂z}(-1,1,1) \\ w+\pi  & =\pi (x+1)-2(y-1)-2(z-1) \\ w+\pi  & =\pi x-2y-2z+4+\pi  \\ \pi x-2y-2z-w+4 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

q-129555.name: Question 11
q-129555.problem: At which point on the surface $z=x\operatorname{ln}⁡y$ is the tangent plane horizontal?
q-129555.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡y \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡y)=\frac{x}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡y,\,\frac{x}{y},\,-1⟩.
$$

Note that the tangent plane is horizontal if and only if the normal vector is vertical. This means that the $x$- and $y$-components of the vector must be $0:$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y=0 \\ \frac{x}{y}=0\end{aligned}
$$

 

From the first equation we get $y=1,$ while the second equation gives $x=0.$ 

Finally, substituting $x=0$ and $y=1$ into our function, we get

$$
z=0\operatorname{ln}⁡1=0.
$$

Therefore, the point where the tangent plane is horizontal is $(0,1,0).$

q-73860.problem: At which points on the surface $z={x}^{3}-3x+{y}^{2}+2y$ is the tangent plane horizontal?
q-73860.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}-3x+{y}^{2}+2y) \\  & =3{x}^{2}-3 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{3}-3x+{y}^{2}+2y) \\  & =2y+2\end{aligned}
$$

 

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨3{x}^{2}-3,\,2y+2,\,-1⟩.
$$

Note that the tangent plane is horizontal if and only if the normal vector is vertical. This means that the $x$- and $y$-components of the vector must be $0:$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}-3=0 \\ 2y+2=0\end{aligned}
$$

 

From the first equation, we get $x=\pm 1$ while the second equation gives $y=-1.$ 

Finally, substituting $x=-1$ and $y=-1$ into our function, we get

$$
z=(-1)^{3}-3(-1)+(-1)^{2}+2(-1)=1.
$$

Substituting $x=1$ and $y=-1$ into our function, we get

$$
z=(1)^{3}-3(1)+(-1)^{2}+2(-1)=-3.
$$

Therefore, the points where the tangent plane is horizontal are $(-1,-1,1)$ and $(1,-1,-3).$

∂f∂x=∂∂x(x3−3x+y2+2y)=3x2−3∂f∂y=∂∂y(x3−3x+y2+2y)=2y+2

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is

⟨3x2−3,2y+2,−1⟩.

{∂f∂x=0∂f∂y=0⟹{3x2−3=02y+2=0

From the first equation, we get x=±1 while the second equation gives y=−1.

Finally, substituting x=−1 and y=−1 into our function, we get

z=(−1)3−3(−1)+(−1)2+2(−1)=1. Substituting x=1 and y=−1 into our function, we get

z=(1)3−3(1)+(−1)2+2(−1)=−3.

Therefore, the points where the tangent plane is horizontal are (−1,−1,1) and (1,−1,−3).

q-73855.problem: At which points on the surface $z={e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$ is the tangent plane horizontal?
q-73855.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}) \\  & ={e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot 2x \\  & =2x{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}) \\  & ={e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot 2y \\  & =2y{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨2x{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}},\,2y{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}},\,-1⟩.
$$

Note that the tangent plane is horizontal if and only if the normal vector is vertical. This means that the $x$- and $y$-components of the vector must be $0:$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}2x{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}=0 \\ 2y{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}=0\end{aligned}
$$

 

From the first equation, we get $x=0$ while the second equation gives $y=0.$ 

Finally, substituting $x=0$ and $y=0$ into our function, we get

$$
z={e}^{{0}^{2}+{0}^{2}}=1.
$$

Therefore, the point where the tangent plane is horizontal is $(0,0,1).$

Question 15

At which points on the surface z=xy−3x+2y−5 is the tangent plane horizontal?

a
(1,1,−5) only
b
(−2,3,1) only
c
(1,1,−5) and (0,1,−3)
d
(0,1,−3) only
e
(−2,3,1) and (1,1,−5)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface z=f(x,y) at the point (x0,y0,z0) on the surface can be written as z−z0=(x−x0)∂f∂x(x0,y0)+(y−y0)∂f∂y(x0,y0), where ⟨∂f∂x(x0,y0),∂f∂y(x0,y0),−1⟩ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives: ∂f∂x=∂∂x(xy−3x+2y−5)=y−3∂f∂y=∂∂y(xy−3x+2y−5)=x+2

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is ⟨y−3,x+2,−1⟩.

Note that the tangent plane is horizontal if and only if the normal vector is vertical. This means that the x- and y-components of the vector must be 0: {∂f∂x=0∂f∂y=0⟹{y−3=0x+2=0

From the second equation we get x=−2, while the first equation gives y=3.

Finally, substituting x=−2 and y=3 into our function, we get z=(−2)(3)−3(−2)+2(3)−5=1.

Therefore, the point where the tangent plane is horizontal is (−2,3,1).
